newsitem.title: USA: U.S. court strikes down San Diego teen curfew.
newsitem.headline: U.S. court strikes down San Diego teen curfew.

text.p: A federal appeals court on Monday struck down a San Diego law that forces youths off the streets at 10 p.m., ruling that the city curfew violated the rights of teens and their parents.

The 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in San Francisco said the city's broad juvenile curfew law violated the constitutional rights of minors and the rights of parents to raise their children without undue government interference.

The San Diego law, enacted in 1947, forbids youths younger than 18 to "loiter, idle, wander, stroll or play" on public streets and other public places after 10 p.m. The law allows exceptions when juveniles are with parents, on emergency errands or returning from work or school.
In 1994 the San Diego City Council adopted a resolution calling for police to aggressively enforce the curfew in a bid to curb youth crime and gang activity in the city.

In response a group of teens and their parents, represented by the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), challenged the law's constitutionality, arguing that the measure banned legitimate nighttime activities, such as meeting with friends, dancing and practicing astronomy.
The ACLU argued the ordinance was the equivalent of "house arrest" for law-abiding people.

In December 1995, a federal judge in San Diego concluded the law was constitutional. But the appeals court Monday reversed the ruling, saying the phrase "loiter, wander, idle, stroll or play" was unconstitutionally vague.

"Clearly San Diego could have enacted a narrower curfew ordinance that would pass constitutional muster," the court said in the ruling. "Its present ordinance is problematic because it does not provide exceptions for many legitimate activities, with or without parental permission."
The city may appeal the decision but could also change the language of the ordinance in order to satisfy the court, Deputy San Diego City Attorney James Chapin said.

The ACLU welcomed the ruling, and said it could have implications far beyond San Diego. "We're very gratified," said attorney Michael Marrinan, who worked with the ACLU on the case. "Any city that has a curfew ordinance would have to look at it very carefully in light of this opinion."
